title: The Weekly Cybers #130
text:
21 August 2026

One-third of a random sample of all web content published since ChatGPT was released shows signs of being written by AI. Around half of US adults use chatbots, including 24% who say they use them daily. So that’s a thing.

I’m not sure I’m happy with this thing. How about you?

Anyway, Meta is in court again, Roblox has been slapped for being slack about kids’ safety again, the big online platforms are being asked to pay for news again, and Australians will be able to opt out of gambling advertising thanks to internet magic. What a week!

Sigh.

If you’re looking for something fun to watch this weekend, you might want to seek out reports from Beijing’s World Robot Conference. Humanoid robots are all the rage these days as you’ve probably noticed, especially in China. Some of them even seem to work.

Rather than banning online gambling advertising entirely, the Australian government will be setting up a register so internet users can opt out of gambling ads, somehow

The register is to be operational within 12 months, and will be funded by a new tax on the gambling companies.

As the Guardian reports, “In the meantime, from 1 January, all online services must provide an opt-out function if they want to display gambling ads. But little is known about how the one-stop opt-out register will operate, with questions about data privacy and how exactly people will be able to use it”.

A single register for opting out would be useful for end users, sure, but adverts arrive on people’s devices via many different routes.

Websites and mobile apps don’t choose which ads they show. Rather, they rely on embedded software from advertising broking platforms, and that software decided on the fly which ads should be shown. That decision is based on both what the brokers know about the end users — identified by cookies planted on their device — and what the advertisers are willing to pay. Every platform will now need to interrogate the register to see whether gambling ads can be shown as part of the mix.

But what if the end users is running anti-tracking technology such as a cookie blockers?

And what about podcasts? Sports podcasts in particular might have gambling ads read by the presenters. Would there now need to be two different versions of the pod, one without the problem ads, with a correctly-chosen version sent to the two different types of users? Once more, this requires the podcast distribution platform to identify individual users.

Come on you nerds, just nerd better and solve the social problem!

Your writer can’t help but think this is another case of the government proposing a solution to a problem, and simply expecting the technology sector to nerd harder and make it happen — just as they did with the teen social media ban, and the much-ridiculed “internet clean feed” of what now seems like a bygone era.

“The government’s legislation leaves the details about how the register will work to the Australian Communications and Media Authority,” writes the Guardian.

The legislation itself consists of the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 and its friend the Interactive Gambling (Cost Recovery Levy) Bill 2026.

Meanwhile, ACMA continues to issue blocking notices to help prevent Australians from seeing overseas gambling websites which would be illegal under Australian law.

DOES SOMETHING IN THE EMAIL LOOK WRONG? Let me know. If there’s ever a factual error, editing mistake, or confusing typo, it’ll be corrected in the web archives.

The Weekly Cybers is a personal weekly digest of what the Australian government has been saying and doing in the digital and cyber realms, on various adjacent topics, and whatever else interests me, Stilgherrian, published every Friday afternoon (nearly).

If I’ve missed anything, or if there’s any specific items you’d like me to follow, please let me know.
